lessons.title: Who our customers are and what they expect
lessons.html:
Customers in the abattoir business

An abattoir serves several kinds of customers. External customers include livestock owners who bring animals for slaughter, butcheries, supermarkets, meat wholesalers, restaurants and private buyers. Internal customers are colleagues in the next section of the process: the slaughter floor serves the chillers, the chillers serve deboning and dispatch. Every person in the chain depends on the quality and timeliness of the work before them.

What customers expect

  • Safe, wholesome meat produced under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000 and the abattoir's hygiene programme.
  • Consistent quality: correct classification, trimming, temperature and presentation.
  • Accuracy: correct carcass weights, identification, invoices and orders.
  • Reliability: delivery or collection at the agreed time.
  • Respectful, competent service: prompt responses, clear information and honesty.
  • Confidentiality of their business information.

Why relationships matter

Customers have choices. A livestock farmer can take animals to another abattoir; a butchery can change suppliers. Keeping an existing customer usually costs far less than finding a new one, and satisfied customers recommend the business to others. A single poor experience, badly handled, can lose a customer and damage the abattoir's reputation in a small farming community.

Understanding customer needs

Find out what each customer actually needs: preferred carcass specifications, delivery days, documentation, payment terms and how they like to be contacted. Record these in the customer file and share them with colleagues who serve that customer. Ask for feedback regularly rather than waiting for complaints.

lessons.title: Communicating, handling complaints and building loyalty
lessons.html:
Professional communication

  • Greet customers promptly and politely, by name where possible.
  • Listen actively: let the customer finish, ask clarifying questions, and summarise what you understood.
  • Give accurate information. If you do not know, say so and find out; never guess about weights, prices or test results.
  • Keep promises. If a delivery will be late, tell the customer before the agreed time, with a new time.
  • Use professional language on the phone, email and WhatsApp. Confirm important agreements in writing.
  • Respect cultural and language differences, and treat all customers equally.

Handling complaints

A complaint is an opportunity to keep a customer. Use a structured approach:

  1. Listen without interrupting or arguing. Stay calm even if the customer is angry.
  2. Acknowledge the problem and thank them for raising it.
  3. Gather facts: what, when, which carcass or order number, and evidence such as photos or temperature records.
  4. Act or refer: resolve it if it is within your authority, otherwise refer it to the responsible person and tell the customer who will contact them and when.
  5. Follow up to confirm the customer is satisfied.
  6. Record the complaint, cause and corrective action, so the problem does not recur.

Never promise what the business cannot deliver, and never blame colleagues in front of a customer.

Example

A butchery reports that carcasses arrived warmer than agreed. The staff member apologises, takes the delivery details, checks chiller and vehicle temperature records with the supervisor, and the abattoir arranges an inspection. The cause, a faulty truck unit, is fixed, and the customer is informed of the corrective action and a credit as authorised by management.

Building long-term loyalty

  • Be consistent: the same high standard every time.
  • Keep customers informed about changes such as public holiday schedules or price changes in good time.
  • Recognise regular customers and their preferences.
  • Act with integrity: never accept bribes or favour one customer unfairly.

Key points

  • Customers include external buyers and livestock owners, and internal colleagues.
  • Customers expect safe meat, consistent quality, accuracy, reliability and respect.
  • Listen actively, give accurate information and keep promises.
  • Handle complaints by listening, acknowledging, gathering facts, acting, following up and recording.
  • Consistency and integrity build long-term loyalty.
